skillDomains.name: Workshop Safety
skillDomains.description: Welding kills careless people. Safety is the first skill, not an afterthought.

skills.name: Personal Protective Equipment
skills.description: The gear that stands between you and serious injury.

modules.title: Why welders wear armour
modules.content:
Welding produces:

  • Ultraviolet light that burns eyes and skin — arc eye is a real injury
  • Molten metal spatter at 1,500°C+
  • Toxic fumes from flux and coatings
  • Noise from grinding and cutting

Every piece of PPE exists because someone got hurt without it. Wear all of it, every time — not even a 30-second tack weld is worth your eyesight.

visuals.title: Full PPE set for arc welding
visuals.description: A labelled image of a welder in complete PPE: auto-darkening helmet, safety glasses, leather gauntlets, welding jacket, high-top steel-toe boots, ear protection, and respirator where required. Callouts explain what each item protects against.
visuals.learningPurpose: Show the learner exactly what full protection looks like before they touch equipment.
visuals.altText: A welder wearing an auto-darkening helmet, safety glasses underneath, leather gauntlets, a leather jacket, high-top steel-toe boots, ear protection, and a respirator.
visuals.caption: Every item has a reason. Learn them before you weld.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Explain the physics of arc flash (UV radiation burns), the temperature of spatter, the composition of welding fumes, and why each PPE item targets a specific injury mechanism — not just 'wear this'.
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Name every PPE item, state what it protects against, and describe the injury that occurs without it.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Ask the learner to correctly put on and inspect their own PPE before any live arc is struck.

learningObjectives: Identify each item of welding PPE and its protective function.
Explain the specific injury each item prevents.
Demonstrate correct donning, fit, and inspection of PPE.
Recognise when PPE is damaged and must be replaced.

assessmentCriteria: Correct PPE selection for the task
All required items worn and correctly fitted
Damaged or non-compliant PPE identified and removed
Verbal explanation of each item's purpose

modules.title: The full PPE checklist
modules.content:
Head and face

  • Welding helmet with correct shade lens (auto-darkening is best)
  • Safety glasses underneath (for chipping slag)
  • Cap under helmet if you have long hair

Body

  • Leather welding jacket or apron
  • Long sleeves, no cuffs (spatter catches in cuffs)
  • Leather gauntlet gloves

Feet

  • Steel-toe leather boots, high-top
  • No open shoes, ever

Respiratory

  • Respirator if welding galvanised, painted, or stainless steel
  • Good ventilation always

visuals.title: Pre-weld PPE inspection checklist
visuals.description: A tick-box visual checklist with icons for each PPE item: helmet, lens shade, safety glasses, gloves, jacket, boots, respirator. Each row has a 'condition' check and an image showing a compliant vs non-compliant item.
visuals.learningPurpose: Turn PPE into a routine inspection so learners never start work without checking.
visuals.altText: A visual PPE inspection checklist with compliant and non-compliant examples for each item.
visuals.caption: Inspect every item before every weld. No exceptions.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Teach that PPE inspection is a discipline, not a ritual. Damaged leather, cracked lenses, and worn boots are silent failures that cause real injuries. Explain the correct helmet shade number for the amperage range being used.
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Walk through the full pre-weld inspection using the checklist and reject any item that fails.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Observe the learner's inspection sequence and confirm they can justify every accept/reject decision.

learningObjectives: Perform a complete pre-weld PPE inspection.
Select the correct helmet shade for the amperage.
Identify when PPE is unsafe to use and must be replaced.
Explain the correct sequence for donning PPE.

assessmentCriteria: Correctly identifies compliant vs non-compliant items
Selects correct lens shade for the task

modules.title: PPE check

steps.q: You're about to tack weld a small joint. Can you skip the helmet?
o: Only if the weld is very small
Only if you close your eyes
steps.f: Arc eye can happen from a single flash. Never skip the helmet.

steps.q: You're welding galvanised steel. What extra protection is required?
steps.f: Galvanised coating releases toxic zinc fumes.

steps.q: You notice your welding jacket sleeve has a hole. What do you do?
steps.f: A hole in leather lets spatter through.

visuals.title: Is this PPE acceptable? Decision flow
visuals.description: A visual decision tree: Is the item clean? Cracked? Burned? Correctly sized? Each branch leads to 'use' or 'replace'. Includes examples of common damage on each PPE type.
visuals.learningPurpose: Build the habit of judging PPE condition in real time.
visuals.altText: A decision flowchart for judging whether each PPE item is acceptable for use.
visuals.caption: The wrong answer here costs skin, eyes, or lungs.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: At this level, learners must justify their PPE decisions against real-world consequences. Discuss case histories of arc eye, metal fume fever, and burn injuries — how each was caused, and what PPE would have prevented it.
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Complete the drill with 90% or higher and explain why each wrong answer is dangerous.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Have the learner walk through the drill out loud, explaining consequences for each wrong option.

learningObjectives: Apply PPE rules under realistic welding scenarios.
Justify acceptance or rejection of PPE based on condition.
Recognise hazards that require additional protection beyond baseline PPE.

assessmentCriteria: Achieves 90% or above on the drill
Explains the injury each wrong option would cause
Correctly identifies when additional PPE is required

skills.name: Fire Prevention
skills.description: Welding sparks travel far. Preventing fires is part of the job.

modules.title: Sparks travel farther than you think
modules.content:
Welding spatter can travel up to 10 metres and stay hot enough to ignite wood, cloth, or fuel for minutes after landing.

Before welding anywhere

  1. Clear a 10-metre radius of anything flammable
  2. Cover what can't be moved with fire blankets
  3. Have a fire extinguisher within arm's reach
  4. Have a bucket of water or sand nearby
  5. Never weld near fuel, gas cylinders, or paint

After welding, stay on site for at least 30 minutes. Smouldering fires take time to show.

visuals.title: 10-metre spatter zone diagram
visuals.description: A top-down diagram showing a welder at the centre, a 10-metre radius marked, and examples of ignition hazards (rags, fuel cans, wooden pallets, painted walls) placed at various distances. Hot spatter paths are visualised as arrow vectors.
visuals.learningPurpose: Make the invisible risk of airborne spatter physically visible.
visuals.altText: A top-down diagram with a 10-metre radius around a welder, showing typical ignition hazards within the zone.
visuals.caption: If it's inside the circle, it can burn.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Explain the physics of spatter: it cools as it travels, but even at 5 metres it can exceed the ignition temperature of common materials. Discuss fire triangle, extinguisher classes (A, B, C, D), and the specific case of welding near fuel — where vapour, not liquid, is the danger.
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Survey a workspace and map every ignition hazard within 10 metres.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Have the learner physically walk a site and point out each hazard with a reason.

learningObjectives: Identify the 10-metre spatter radius and its implications.
Survey a workspace for ignition hazards before welding.
Select the correct fire extinguisher class for the hazard.
Explain the post-weld 30-minute watch period.

assessmentCriteria: Correctly maps all hazards within 10 metres
Explains the fire triangle for each hazard
Commits to the post-weld watch period

modules.title: React to a fire
modules.prompt: You're welding in a client's workshop. Sparks have ignited a small fire in a pile of rags 3 metres away. Walk through exactly what you do.
modules.context: Small fires become large fires in under 60 seconds.
rubric: Stops welding immediately and turns off equipment
Assesses whether it's small enough to fight or needs evacuation
Uses correct extinguisher type (dry powder or CO2 for electrical areas)
Aims at the base of the fire, not the flames
Evacuates if the fire grows or smoke becomes thick
Calls for help and clears other people away
Reports to client and documents the incident

visuals.title: Fire response decision tree
visuals.description: A visual flowchart: fire discovered → size assessment → fight or evacuate → correct extinguisher → aim at base → sweep → report. Includes visual cues for when a fire is too large to fight (chest height, spreading, smoke build-up).
visuals.learningPurpose: Give the learner a decision path they can recall under pressure.
visuals.altText: A fire response flowchart from discovery through extinguisher use or evacuation.
visuals.caption: Assess fast. Act faster.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Discuss the physiological response to sudden fire (tunnel vision, freezing) and why a rehearsed decision path matters. Explain PASS technique (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep) and the physical signs that a fire is beyond single-person response: heat on the face, chest-high flames, smoke at ceiling level.
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Walk through the flowchart for the given scenario and justify each decision.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Have the learner explain what would change if the fire were at 5 metres, in a fuel can, or under a bench.

learningObjectives: Apply the fire response decision tree under pressure.
Distinguish fightable from un-fightable fires.
Demonstrate correct extinguisher technique (PASS).
Report and document welding fires correctly.

diplomaPracticals.title: Safety: PPE and fire prevention — supervised demonstration
diplomaPracticals.prompt: Demonstrate correct PPE selection, inspection, and fire prevention preparation for a real welding task. Complete a full pre-weld safety check under instructor observation.

steps.title: Prepare
steps.instruction: Inspect all PPE. Reject any damaged item. Lay out fire prevention equipment (extinguisher, water, sand).
steps.visual: Illustrated PPE and fire equipment layout

steps.title: Survey
steps.instruction: Walk the workspace and identify every ignition hazard within 10 metres. Document with a sketch or photo.

steps.title: Control
steps.instruction: Clear, cover, or remove every hazard. Explain each action as you do it.

steps.title: Verify
steps.instruction: Confirm extinguisher pressure, accessibility, and correct class. Confirm water/sand location.

steps.title: Reflect
steps.instruction: Record what you would do differently on the next job. Note any hazards you initially missed.

visuals.title: Full practical walkthrough: Safety preparation
visuals.description: Five-stage visual walkthrough covering PPE inspection, hazard survey, control actions, verification, and reflection.
visuals.learningPurpose: Let the learner rehearse the full safety workflow visually before performing it.
visuals.altText: Five illustrated stages of a supervised safety preparation practical.
visuals.caption: Follow the stages in order and ask the instructor to verify each safety-critical step.

skillDomains.name: Metal Preparation
skillDomains.description: A weld is only as good as the preparation.

skills.name: Reading Drawings
skills.description: Interpret technical drawings and welding symbols.

modules.title: Drawings are a language
modules.content:
Before you cut a single piece of metal, you must read the drawing. A drawing tells you:

  • Dimensions of every piece
  • Type of weld required at each joint
  • Materials and thickness
  • Any special notes

Misreading a drawing wastes metal and time — and can produce a structurally unsound product.

visuals.title: Anatomy of a welding drawing
visuals.description: A real technical drawing of a steel frame with labelled callouts: dimensions, weld symbols, material notes, title block, and revision history. Each label points to the exact location on the drawing.
visuals.learningPurpose: Show the learner what to look at when opening a drawing for the first time.
visuals.altText: A technical welding drawing with labelled callouts for dimensions, weld symbols, materials, and title block.
visuals.caption: Every drawing has the same information. Learn where to look.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Explain the drafting conventions: first-angle vs third-angle projection, dimension lines vs extension lines, and how the title block tells you the scale and revision. Discuss what happens when a drawing is misread on a structural job.
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Identify each labelled element on the drawing and explain what it tells the fabricator.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Have the learner explain the difference between a dimension line and an extension line.

learningObjectives: Identify the main components of a technical welding drawing.
Explain what each component communicates.
Understand scale and revision control.
Recognise the difference between first- and third-angle projection.

modules.title: The five welding symbols you must know
modules.content:
1. Fillet weld (triangle)

The most common weld. Joins two pieces at a right angle.

2. Butt weld (straight line)

Joins two pieces end-to-end.

3. Square butt

Simple edge-to-edge without bevel.

4. V-groove (V shape)

Pieces are beveled to allow deeper penetration.

5. Weld-all-around (circle at joint)

Means weld the entire circumference.

Numbers next to symbols indicate leg length or weld size in millimetres.

visuals.title: Five core welding symbols chart
visuals.description: A reference chart showing each of the five symbols drawn as they appear on a drawing, alongside a real-world photograph of the joint they produce. The weld size and length notation is annotated.
visuals.learningPurpose: Give the learner a single reference image they can return to for every symbol.
visuals.altText: A chart of five welding symbols with real photographs of the joints they specify.
visuals.caption: Symbol on the left, actual weld on the right.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Explain where the size number goes (left of symbol for fillet leg length, above the line for groove weld size), where the length number goes, and what a tail annotation means (process specification). Discuss the difference between a symbol placed above the reference line vs below.
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Read each symbol on a drawing and describe the resulting joint before seeing the photograph.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Have the learner sketch the joint each symbol produces without looking.

learningObjectives: Identify the five core welding symbols on any drawing.
Interpret size and length notation.
Explain where the weld is applied (arrow side vs other side).
Match a symbol to the actual joint it specifies.

assessmentCriteria: Sketches correct joint for each symbol

modules.title: Read the symbols

steps.q: A drawing shows a triangle with a '6' next to it at a corner joint. What does this mean?
steps.f: Triangle = fillet weld. The number indicates leg length in mm.

steps.q: A symbol shows a circle at the joint between two pieces. What does this mean?
steps.f: The circle at the joint means weld the full perimeter.

steps.q: A drawing shows a V shape at the joint. Why is the V there?
o: The pieces are beveled to allow deeper weld penetration
steps.f: A V-groove is prepared so the weld penetrates the full thickness.

visuals.title: Symbol to joint — before and after
visuals.description: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, the drawn symbol as it appears on a technical drawing; on the right, a photograph of the finished weld on the actual joint. Numbered to match each drill question.
visuals.learningPurpose: Train the eye to translate from drawing to metal without guessing.
visuals.altText: Side-by-side drawings of weld symbols and photographs of the resulting welds.
visuals.caption: The symbol predicts the weld. Read it correctly.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Require the learner to read symbols on real drawings from real jobs — not just answer drill questions. Discuss how a misread symbol on a structural drawing leads to over-welding (wasted cost) or under-welding (dangerous).
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Achieve 90%+ on the drill and then read three real drawings with a supervisor.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Verify the learner's reading of an unlabelled drawing.

learningObjectives: Interpret welding symbols under time pressure.
Translate symbol to weld without intermediate steps.
Catch ambiguous or incorrect symbols on a drawing.

assessmentCriteria: Achieves 90% or above on the drill
Correctly reads three real drawings with instructor present
Identifies any errors or ambiguities on the drawings

skills.name: Cleaning & Fit-Up
skills.description: Clean metal welds well. Dirty metal welds badly.

modules.title: The invisible enemy: contamination
modules.content:
Weld contamination comes from:

  • Rust
  • Mill scale (the dark coating on new steel)
  • Oil and grease
  • Paint
  • Moisture

All of these cause:

  • Porosity (holes in the weld)
  • Poor penetration
  • Cracking
  • Weak joints

Clean metal is the foundation of a strong weld.

visuals.title: Contaminated vs clean weld comparison
visuals.description: A split image: on the left, a weld on dirty metal showing visible porosity and rough surface; on the right, a weld on clean metal showing smooth, defect-free finish. Both welds done by the same welder, same settings.
visuals.learningPurpose: Prove that preparation, not skill, is the difference.
visuals.altText: Two welds side by side, one on contaminated metal showing porosity and one on clean metal showing a smooth finish.
visuals.caption: Same welder. Same settings. Different preparation.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Explain metallurgy at a practical level: mill scale is iron oxide; oil and grease vaporise and form gas pockets; moisture produces hydrogen-induced cracking. Each contaminant has a distinct failure mechanism. Teach the learner to identify each visually and by feel.
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Inspect three metal samples and identify the contaminant on each.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Have the learner explain the failure mechanism for each contaminant.

learningObjectives: Identify common weld contaminants visually.
Explain the failure mechanism for each contaminant.
Describe why contaminated welds fail.
Recognise the visual signs of contamination-related defects.

modules.title: Preparation sequence

steps.q: You receive newly cut steel from the supplier. First step?
o: Clean edges of mill scale, rust, and oil
steps.f: New steel has mill scale and cutting oils.

steps.q: There's light surface rust on the joint area. What do you do?
o: Grind or wire-brush to bare metal

steps.q: After cleaning, the two pieces don't fit flush. What do you do?
o: Grind or cut to fit properly
Use more weld to fill the gap

visuals.title: Metal preparation workflow
visuals.description: A four-stage illustrated workflow: 1) inspect for contaminants, 2) clean to bare metal, 3) check fit-up, 4) tack and verify. Each stage shows the acceptable and unacceptable result.
visuals.learningPurpose: Establish the correct sequence so learners never skip a stage.
visuals.altText: Four illustrated stages of metal preparation from inspection to tacking.
visuals.caption: Skipping any stage causes a defect you can't fix later.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Discuss grind direction (cross cuts vs along the joint), correct flap disc and wire brush selection for different metals, and how to check fit-up with a square and feeler gauges. Explain why fit-up matters structurally, not just aesthetically.
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Complete the drill at 90%+ and then demonstrate the sequence on real metal.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Observe preparation on a real joint and grade against the sequence.

learningObjectives: Follow the correct preparation sequence.
Select the correct cleaning tools for each contaminant.
Check fit-up accurately with the appropriate instruments.
Recognise when a joint is ready for welding.

assessmentCriteria: Achieves 90% or above on the drill
Demonstrates correct sequence on real metal
Joint is clean and correctly fitted

skillDomains.name: Welding Techniques
skillDomains.description: The core skill: joining metal with heat and filler.

skills.name: Arc Welding (SMAW)
skills.description: Stick welding — the workhorse of West African workshops.

modules.title: What is arc welding?
modules.content:
Arc welding (also called stick welding or SMAW — Shielded Metal Arc Welding) uses an electrical arc between a consumable electrode and the metal to create heat and melt both the electrode and the workpiece together.

Why it's everywhere in West Africa

  • Equipment is cheap and durable
  • Works outdoors, in wind and rain
  • No gas cylinders needed
  • One machine handles many metals

If you can arc weld well, you can find work anywhere.

visuals.title: SMAW circuit and arc anatomy
visuals.description: A labelled diagram showing the welding machine, electrode holder, workpiece, ground clamp, and the electrical circuit between them. The arc zone is magnified to show molten pool, slag covering, and base metal fusion.
visuals.learningPurpose: Make the invisible circuit and arc visible.
visuals.altText: A diagram of a SMAW welding circuit with the arc zone magnified to show the molten pool and slag.
visuals.caption: Follow the current. Understand the arc.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Explain AC vs DC welding current, electrode positive vs negative, and how polarity affects penetration and deposition rate. Discuss the electrode coating's role: shielding gas generation, slag formation, arc stabilisation, and alloying elements.
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Trace the electrical circuit and name each component.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Have the learner explain the difference between AC and DC welding and when each is used.

learningObjectives: Describe the SMAW process and its electrical circuit.
Explain the function of electrode coating.
Distinguish AC and DC welding and their applications.
Identify the major components of a stick welding setup.

modules.title: Setting the machine
modules.content:
Amperage by electrode diameter

  • 2.5mm electrode → 70–90A
  • 3.2mm electrode → 100–130A
  • 4.0mm electrode → 130–180A
  • 5.0mm electrode → 180–240A

By metal thickness

  • Thin sheet (1–2mm) → lower amps, 2.5mm rod, faster travel
  • Medium (3–6mm) → 3.2mm rod, moderate amps
  • Thick (6mm+) → 4.0mm+ rod, high amps, may need multiple passes

Get amperage wrong and: too low = sticking rod, no penetration. Too high = burn-through, spatter, undercut.

visuals.title: Amperage selection chart by electrode and thickness
visuals.description: A dual-axis chart: electrode diameter on one axis, metal thickness on the other. Each cell shows the recommended amperage range. Colour coding: green = correct zone, yellow = risky, red = wrong. Includes photos of the resulting weld at correct, too-low, and too-high amperage.
visuals.learningPurpose: Give the learner a visual reference so settings become intuition.
visuals.altText: A chart showing correct amperage for electrode diameter and metal thickness with weld photo examples.
visuals.caption: Match the rod, the thickness, and the amps — every time.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Explain the relationship between amperage, arc length, and heat input. Discuss arc force and how it affects penetration. Teach the learner to read the weld appearance as feedback: is it too cold (roped, high crown), too hot (undercut, burn-through), or correct (smooth, even, slight crown)?
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Select correct settings for three different metal thicknesses.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Have the learner set up the machine and justify every setting before striking an arc.

learningObjectives: Select correct amperage for a given electrode and thickness.
Explain the relationship between amperage and heat input.
Recognise the visual signs of correct, too-cold, and too-hot welding.
Adjust settings based on observed weld quality.

assessmentCriteria: Correctly selects settings for three thicknesses
Justifies each setting based on the chart

modules.title: Diagnose arc welding problems

steps.q: The electrode keeps sticking to the workpiece. Most likely cause?
steps.f: Low amperage doesn't create enough heat to keep the arc going.

steps.q: You see 'undercut' — a groove melted into the base metal beside the weld. Cause?
o: Amperage too high or travel too fast
steps.f: Undercut comes from too much heat input or moving too fast.

steps.q: The weld has small holes in it (porosity). What's the most likely cause?

visuals.title: Weld defect diagnosis gallery
visuals.description: A gallery of weld photographs, each labelled with the defect (porosity, undercut, spatter, cold lap, burn-through) and matched to the cause and corrective action. Allows side-by-side comparison of correct vs defective welds.
visuals.learningPurpose: Train the eye to diagnose by appearance.
visuals.altText: A gallery of weld photographs showing common defects and their correct counterparts.
visuals.caption: Learn the defect. Learn the cause. Learn the fix.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Move beyond surface-level defect identification. Explain how each defect affects structural integrity: porosity reduces cross-section, undercut creates stress concentration, cold lap means no fusion. Discuss the standards (ISO 5817, AWS D1.1) that specify acceptable limits.
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Diagnose defects on real weld samples without looking at the answers.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Have the learner explain what process correction would fix each defect.

learningObjectives: Diagnose common weld defects by visual inspection.
Identify the process parameters that cause each defect.
Explain how each defect affects structural integrity.
State the corrective action for each defect.

assessmentCriteria: Achieves 90% or above on the drill
Correctly diagnoses defects on real samples
Explains cause and correction for each

modules.title: Weld a critical joint
modules.prompt: You need to weld a 6mm steel plate butt joint that will carry significant load. Describe your approach — preparation, settings, technique, and post-weld inspection.
modules.context: Structural welds must be correct. The consequences of failure are injury or death.
rubric: Cleans and bevels the joint edges
Sets machine for 3.2mm or 4.0mm rod at correct amps
Tacks the joint first to prevent distortion
Runs a root pass, then fill passes if needed
Maintains consistent travel speed and angle
Inspects for porosity, undercut, cracks
May consider a cap pass for appearance and strength

visuals.title: Structural butt joint — pass sequence
visuals.description: A cross-section diagram of a 6mm butt joint showing: root pass with correct penetration, fill pass, and cap pass. Each pass labelled with its function, amperage, and rod size. Defect examples shown alongside for comparison.
visuals.learningPurpose: Show how a multi-pass structural weld is built up.
visuals.altText: A cross-section diagram of a multi-pass butt weld showing root, fill, and cap passes.
visuals.caption: Every pass has a purpose.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Explain the metallurgy of multi-pass welding: interpass temperature control, heat-affected zone (HAZ), and residual stress. Discuss when a welded joint needs pre-heat or post-heat treatment. This is the moment to introduce the difference between a good-looking weld and a structurally sound one.
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Plan the weld sequence for the scenario, then execute it on scrap plate.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Review the plan against the drawing and inspect the finished weld.

learningObjectives: Plan a multi-pass weld sequence for a structural joint.
Execute a butt weld with correct penetration.
Perform post-weld visual inspection.
Explain the difference between cosmetic and structural quality.

assessmentCriteria: Plan includes preparation, settings, sequence, and inspection
Executed weld shows correct penetration and profile

skills.name: Joint Types
skills.description: The five fundamental joints every welder must master.

modules.title: The five joints
modules.content:
1. Butt joint

Two pieces end-to-end. Used for lengthening, repairing.

2. Corner joint

Two pieces meeting at 90° forming an L. Used for boxes, frames.

3. T-joint

One piece perpendicular to another. Used for structural frameworks.

4. Lap joint

Two pieces overlapping. Used for sheet metal, panels.

5. Edge joint

Two pieces joined along their edges. Used for thin sheet.

Every welded structure is a combination of these five.

visuals.title: The five joint types — cross-section and real photos
visuals.description: A reference chart: for each of the five joint types, a cross-section diagram showing the weld placement, followed by a real photograph of the completed joint in metal. Labels identify the plates and weld.
visuals.learningPurpose: Give the learner one reference image they can return to for every joint.
visuals.altText: A chart showing cross-sections and photographs of the five fundamental weld joints.
visuals.caption: Every structure is a combination of these five.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Explain where each joint is used in real structures: butt joints for plates and pipe runs, T-joints for beams to columns, lap joints for sheet metal and tanks, corner joints for frames and boxes. Discuss which joints take tensile vs shear load and why that matters for weld placement.
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Name each joint type and one real-world application for each.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Have the learner identify joints in a real structure photograph.

learningObjectives: Identify the five fundamental joint types.

assessmentCriteria: Names a real application for each

skills.name: Inspection & Quality
skills.description: Judge your own work against real standards.

modules.title: Weld inspection basics
modules.content:
Every weld should be visually inspected before the job is considered done. Look for:

  • Cracks — anything remotely looking like a crack is a rejection
  • Porosity — small holes, indicates contamination
  • Undercut — melted groove beside the weld, weakens the joint
  • Incomplete fusion — weld doesn't stick to the base metal
  • Slag inclusions — trapped slag inside the weld
  • Spatter — cosmetic but unprofessional if excessive

Structural and pressure welds require professional NDT (non-destructive testing) — X-ray, ultrasonic, or dye penetrant.

visuals.title: Weld defect identification gallery
visuals.description: A visual reference chart showing each weld defect: crack, porosity, undercut, incomplete fusion, slag inclusion, and excess spatter. Each defect is paired with a close-up photograph and a short description of why it matters.
visuals.learningPurpose: Give the learner the vocabulary and visuals for every common defect.
visuals.altText: A chart showing photographs of each common weld defect with descriptions.
visuals.caption: Every defect has a name and a cause.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Explain the difference between visual inspection and NDT. Discuss what each NDT method (dye penetrant, magnetic particle, ultrasonic, X-ray) detects and where each is required by code. Teach the learner that not all defects are visible to the eye — but the ones that are must always be caught.
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Identify each defect type in a set of weld photographs.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Have the learner sort weld samples by defect type without prompts.

learningObjectives: Identify the six most common weld defects visually.
Explain how each defect compromises the weld.
Distinguish visual inspection from NDT methods.
Apply acceptance criteria for structural welds.

assessmentCriteria: Explains how each defect affects the weld

modules.title: Accept or reject

steps.q: You see a small crack running along the edge of a weld. Action?
steps.f: Any crack is a serious defect. Grind it out completely and re-weld.

steps.q: You see light porosity (small holes) in a non-structural fence weld. Action?
o: Grind and re-weld if time allows; note to client
steps.f: Non-structural porosity is often acceptable, but professional welders still fix it when possible.

steps.q: You see undercut along a structural weld. Action?
o: Grind and re-weld — undercut weakens the joint
steps.f: Undercut reduces the cross-section of the base metal.

visuals.title: Accept / reject decision chart
visuals.description: A decision flowchart for weld inspection: defect identified → structural or non-structural → defect type → accept, rework, or reject. Each terminal state shows the required action.
visuals.learningPurpose: Give the learner a decision path they can apply on the job.
visuals.altText: A decision flowchart for accepting, reworking, or rejecting a weld based on defect type and application.
visuals.caption: Not every defect is equal. Know the difference.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Explain the acceptance criteria from real codes: ISO 5817 quality levels B, C, D; AWS D1.1 acceptance criteria for different weld types. Discuss the difference between cosmetic defects (spatter) and structural defects (cracks, lack of fusion).
teachingNotes.learnerTask: Apply the flowchart to 10 photographed weld samples and defend each decision.
teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Have the learner defend each accept/reject decision against the code.

learningObjectives: Apply acceptance criteria consistently.

assessmentCriteria: Achieves 90% or above on the drill
Defends each decision with code reference

skills.name: Estimating & Pricing
skills.description: Quote jobs correctly and never lose money on a weld.

modules.title: How to price a welding job
modules.content:
Every welding quote covers:

  1. Materials — steel, electrodes, gas, consumables
  2. Labour — your time at a real hourly rate
  3. Overhead — electricity, transport, tool wear
  4. Profit — the margin that keeps you in business

Most beginner welders only quote materials + a little. Then they wonder why they're broke.

Price = (Materials + Labour + Overhead) × (1 + Margin)

A 25–40% margin is standard for small fabrication work.

visuals.title: Four-part pricing flowchart
visuals.description: A visual pricing model: the four components (materials, labour, overhead, margin) flow into a base cost, which flows through a margin multiplier to a final price. Includes worked example with numbers.
visuals.learningPurpose: Make pricing a system, not a guess.
visuals.altText: A pricing flowchart showing how materials, labour, overhead, and margin combine to produce a final price.
visuals.caption: Every component must be counted.

teachingNotes.diplomaDepth: Discuss the cost structure of a fabrication business: fixed vs variable costs, the true cost of your time, and the danger of competing on price alone. Explain how to justify a fair price to a client who is comparing quotes.

teachingNotes.instructorCheck: Review each pricing calculation and challenge any missing component.

implementationNotes: Build a visual asset for every learning item. Do not rely on a single hero image for an entire module.
Use real, properly consented welding demonstrations where possible; otherwise create original labelled diagrams or licensed assets.
For video assets, include a short transcript, chapter/step markers, and captions.
Keep image and video URLs in a separate asset manifest once actual media is available; do not fabricate URLs.
Render diagrams responsively for mobile screens and low-bandwidth users; offer compressed still images and text alternatives.
Use Sierra Leone-relevant fabrication examples and local currency (Le) where appropriate, but verify current material costs before publication.
Use an instructor-approved safety protocol and local workplace-safety guidance for PPE, ventilation, fire prevention, and incident response.
A visual should teach a specific skill: labels, arrows, stages, comparison, or decision points must be meaningful and readable.
Instructors must inspect every learner weld before it leaves the workshop, both for quality and for safety-critical defects.
